title: Latitude & Longitude Basics
summary: Latitude = how far north/south of the equator; longitude = how far east/west of the Prime Meridian.
quick_actions: Latitude lines run east-west and measure 0° (equator) to 90° N or S at the poles.
Longitude lines run north-south (pole to pole) and measure 0° (Prime Meridian, through Greenwich, UK) to 180° E or W.
Coordinates are always written latitude first, then longitude (e.g. 40.7128° N, 74.0060° W).
A minus sign is a common shorthand for S or W (e.g. -74.0060 means 74.0060° W).
more_info: Every point on Earth's surface has a unique latitude/longitude pair - this is the basis every other coordinate format (DMS, UTM, MGRS) is built on or converts to/from.

title: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)
summary: The same location can be written several different ways - know which one your device/map uses.
quick_actions: Decimal Degrees (DD): e.g. 38.5, -98.30 - the format most phone GPS apps show by default.
Degrees Minutes Seconds (DMS): e.g. 42°30'00" N, 98°15'30" W - each degree splits into 60 minutes, each minute into 60 seconds.
UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator): divides the world into 60 numbered zones, position given as an easting/northing in meters - common on USGS topographic maps.
MGRS (Military Grid Reference System): the same UTM grid, but identifies the 100km square with letters instead of numbers - common on military/tactical maps.
more_info: To convert DD to DMS: the whole number is degrees; multiply the decimal part by 60 for minutes; multiply the leftover decimal by 60 again for seconds. All formats describe the same underlying grid - they're just different notations for it.

title: How GPS Works Without Internet
summary: GPS gets your position from satellites directly - it never needed the internet or cell service.
quick_actions: A GPS receiver listens for timing signals broadcast by satellites - it doesn't send or receive anything over the internet or cell network to compute a position.
At least 4 satellites in view are needed for a full 3D position fix (latitude, longitude, and elevation).
The US maintains at least 24 operational GPS satellites at all times, so several are visible from almost anywhere on Earth at any time.
What DOES need the internet/cell data: downloading new map tiles, live traffic, or searching for an address by name - the position fix itself does not.
more_info: This is why a phone in airplane mode (with GPS/location services left on) can still show your coordinates and a pre-downloaded map with no signal at all - only fetching new map data or looking up a place by name requires connectivity.

title: Cardinal Directions & Compass Bearings
summary: N/E/S/W at 90° intervals; a bearing is the clockwise angle from north to your target.
quick_actions: Cardinal directions: North 0°, East 90°, South 180°, West 270°.
Intercardinal directions sit halfway between: Northeast 45°, Southeast 135°, Southwest 225°, Northwest 315°.
A compass bearing is the clockwise angle from north to wherever you're pointing/heading.

Check current magnetic declination for your area (ngdc.noaa.gov/geomag) before navigating by compass bearing - a map's 'true north' and a compass's 'magnetic north' can differ enough to send you well off course.
more_info: Magnetic declination varies by location and changes slowly over time, so a fixed number memorized once can become inaccurate years later - check it for your actual area when it matters.

title: Basic Offline Navigation Concepts
summary: A paper map, a compass, and knowing your last confirmed position go a long way with zero electronics.
quick_actions: Orient the map: align it so north on the paper points to actual north (using a compass, or the sun near local noon in the Northern Hemisphere as a rough check).

Dead reckoning: estimate your current position from a known starting point plus the direction and distance you've traveled since - simple, but errors add up the longer you go without checking a landmark.
Use terrain/landmarks (a distinct hill, river bend, or intersection) to confirm your estimated position whenever you can - don't rely on dead reckoning alone for long stretches.

A GPS device or phone (see How GPS Works Without Internet) can give you an exact coordinate to place on a paper map even with zero cell/Wi-Fi signal, combining the reliability of electronics with the resilience of paper.
more_info: None of this requires memorizing survival techniques - the practical takeaway is: carry a paper map of your area as a backup, know roughly how to read it, and treat GPS coordinates and paper maps as complementary, not either/or.
